title: verdict
description: The grader's output, produced under constrained decoding. FIELD ORDER IS LOAD-BEARING: the model emits fields in schema order, so the order here is the order it is forced to think in. `claims` comes first so technical content is extracted BEFORE any score exists to rationalise towards - the correctness penalty measured against non-native phrasing is the reason, since a grader scoring correctness straight from a transcript is scoring the prose and the claims together. Within a dimension the same principle applies: evidence, then reasoning, then score. `recommendation` is deliberately absent: it is a pure function of `overall`, and asking the model for it produced strong_yes on candidates scored 2 of 5 in two runs. Constrained decoding guarantees shape, not coherence between fields - every enum value satisfies the schema. It is derived in code.

claims.description: Every checkable technical assertion the candidate made, extracted before anything is scored. Restate each one plainly in your own words - stripping the phrasing is the point, because a claim is true or false independently of how fluently it was said.

claim.description: The assertion, restated plainly. Not a quote: a quote carries the phrasing back in, which is what this field exists to remove.

status.description: Judge the technical content only. `unverifiable` is for claims about the candidate's own history, which cannot be checked and must not be counted as either right or wrong.

evidence.description: Quote or closely paraphrase what the candidate actually said. Write this before deciding a score.

reasoning.description: How that evidence maps to the rubric.

score.description: Integer from 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent). Must follow from the evidence above. For correctness, score the claims list: how many are `correct` against how many are `incorrect`. Phrasing, grammar and fluency are not evidence about correctness and must not move this number.
